name: Aquatic / marine fragrances

lead: Aquatic or marine fragrances are a perfume family that aims to smell like sea air, spray and clean water. Their signature ingredient is Calone, a synthetic molecule with a watery, melon-like, ozone-tinged scent.

People wear them to project freshness and cleanliness, which feeds into the overall grooming impression alongside skin, hair and clothing. The family took off in the 1990s and remains a staple of department-store and designer men's fragrance.

paras: Wearers apply them as a regular daily cologne, often as a light, warm-weather or gym-to-office scent. Many layer them with matching body wash or deodorant, and the sharp, clean character is commonly paired with a short, tidy grooming routine.
The main risks are ordinary fragrance ones: skin irritation or allergic reaction in sensitive people and headaches from strong scents. Calone itself is listed as an irritant in concentrated form.

chain: Smell clean and crisp to people nearby
Adds to the overall well-groomed impression
angle.text: A marine scent is part of how someone comes across in close contact. People choose it for a clean, easy-to-wear signature that complements the rest of their grooming.

lead: Aquatic or marine fragrances are a scent family built to evoke the sea, wet stone, ozone and clean water. The key ingredient is Calone (methylbenzodioxepinone), a compound discovered at Pfizer in 1966 that perfumers use for an intense sea-breeze note with slight floral and fruity overtones [1].

In looksmaxxing terms, a fresh scent is a cheap, reversible way to add to the impression of being well kept. Wearers choose aquatic scents for a clean, approachable signature that sits naturally alongside skincare, haircare and clothing choices.
Calone has been used in perfumery since the 1980s and became a dominant note in marine-style perfumes from the 1990s [1].

paras: Perfumers use Calone to suggest a fresh seashore, with watery, clean, melon, green, marine and ozone facets [1]. Its structure resembles the pheromones of brown algae such as ectocarpene [1].

Pfizer discovered Calone in 1966 [1]. It has been used in perfumery since the 1980s and became a more dominant note in marine-trend perfumes starting in the 1990s [1]. The Swiss company Firmenich later released an isopropyl homologue under the brand name Cascalone [1].
Within grooming communities, aquatic scents are usually discussed as an easy, inoffensive option for daily and warm-weather wear, and as a way to smell clean after a gym session or shower.
Calone is listed as an irritant [1]. As with other fragrances, individual sensitivity to perfume ingredients varies.

timeline.event: Marine-trend perfumes make Calone a dominant note [1].
